newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Critics blast Slovenian referendum as farce.
newsitem.headline: Critics blast Slovenian referendum as farce.

text.p: Slovenian voters failed to back changes to the electoral system in the first referendum in Slovenia since independence from Yugoslavia, criticised on Monday as a farce and waste of money.
With 98.4 percent of votes counted from Sunday's referendum, it was clear none of the three electoral models put forward in the ballot had won the necessary 50 percent support to be adopted.

Little more than a third of the 1.5 million electorate bothered to take part in the referendum. Turnout of around 38 percent was the lowest in a nationwide ballot since Slovenia declared independence in 1991.
Turnout in a general election last month was 73.7 percent.

"The truth is that the existing electoral system received the large majority of votes in the form of non-participation in the referendum," Igor Luksic, professor of politics at Ljubljana University, told Reuters.
"My opinion is that the main reason for such a low turnout was that most voters considered the referendum to be a big farce," Luksic added.
The state statistical office said that the latest unofficial results showed most support for a two-round majority system proposed by the centre-right Social Democrats at 44.4 percent.
Under this model, a candidate would need to secure an absolute majority in two rounds of voting to win each of Slovenia's 88 voting districts.
Such a system would probably have produced a clearer outcome than the inconclusive result of the November 10 general election, which ushered in a period of political uncertainty.

A right-wing alliance failed to win an absolute parliamentary majority by just one seat. Acting Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats remained the biggest party, but are now struggling to find enough support to form a new coalition government.
Dun & Bradstreet credit rating agency on Monday put Slovenia just behind the Czech Republic and ahead of Poland in its December rating report, but said:
"Following the inconclusive results of the general election...it remains unclear whether Slovenia's political stability will remain fully intact."
In the referendum, the Liberal Democrats won just 26.3 percent for their proposal for proportional representation, in which each party would put up a list of 88 candidates.

The third choice on the ballot won 14.4 percent backing. This model combined the Social Democrat and LDS models, with half of the 88 candidates elected on the basis of a two-round run-off system and the rest by proportional representation.
About four percent of those who took the trouble to cast a ballot voted against all three models.

The referendum is expected to cost the country 400 million tolars ($28.6 million) and came at a time when politicians are warning that welfare payments are likely to be cut if Slovenia is to make the grade for European Union membership by 2001.
"The referendum did nothing but...make a fool of voters for their own money," a commentary in Delo newspaper said.
The final official result will be announced on Thursday.
